newsitem.title: ANDORRA: SOCCER-ANDORRA TAKE FIRST STEP ON TRAIL TO FOOTBALLING PEAKS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ANDORRA TAKE FIRST STEP ON TRAIL TO FOOTBALLING PEAKS.

text.p: A tiny mountainous country best known for skiing and duty-free shopping is set to become Europe's latest footballing nation.

Andorra, which is sandwiched into a Pyrenean valley between France and Spain and has no currency or even head of state of its own, makes its debut on Wednesday in a friendly against another recent arrival, Estonia.
But the chances of Andorra producing any upsets are slim -- the country has no professional league and fewer than 300 registered players.
And the national side sounds more like a jury than a team.
Bank clerks, civil servants, accountants, salesmen, construction workers, a lift repairman, an electrician and a hotel manager will line up against Estonia.
It is an amateur spirit echoed by David Carpa, general secretary of the Andorra Football Federation.
"The result is the least important thing...participating is the thing," says Carpa "The players accept beforehand that they are not as well-trained as their opponents."
Even so the game has generated enormous interest amongst the 64,000 inhabitants of Andorra, of whom only 19,000 are actually Andorran, or 'Andorrano'.
"There is a lot of euphoria, a lot of expectation," said Carpa, who anticipates a full house of 1,000 spectators.

About half the population are Spanish, while there are also sizeable Portuguese and French communities in a country where most people speak both Spanish and French in addition to the native Catalan tongue.

Nor can the country absorb players from local club side FC Andorra -- which is largely composed of Spaniards and plays in the Spanish third division -- as 25 years residence is necessary for naturalisation and double nationality is prohibited.

One FC Andorra player, Felix Alvarez, is awaiting permission from FIFA to play with a temporary passport after marrying a local girl. Former Barcelona striker Julio Lucendo, who now plays for the Catalan side Tremp, is in a similar position.
Also missing from the country's debut will be Andorra's joint heads of state -- the bishop of the Spanish town of la Seu d'Urgell and the President of France.
Nor will there be any UEFA chiefs, although they have nevertheless promised to attend an Andorra game in the future.

Andorra joined both FIFA and UEFA in June. The national side hopes to play in the next European championship while local clubs are waiting for a UEFA decision over their admission to continental competitions next season.
But financial restraints may restrict any international ambitions, as the federation has an annual budget of only about eight million pesetas ($62,500).
But Carpa is undaunted.
"Look what the Faroe Islands have done," he says "This will really help the country, it will be good publicity."

Meanwhile Estonia, a team which also tends to produce more problems on team secretaries' maps than on trainer's blackboards, will be in the unaccustomed position of starting a game as firm favourites.
But in the future the people of Andorra could find themselves up against a world footballing power.
"If it's like this before we play Estonia, imagine what it would be like if England or West Germany came," Carpa said.
